overview:
In July 1944, while the war in Europe was still being fought, delegates from forty-four Allied and associated nations gathered at a resort hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, for what was formally called the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference. They met for three weeks and, on 22 July, adopted the Articles of Agreement establishing two new institutions: the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, which later became the core of the World Bank. The problem they were trying to solve was the memory of the 1930s — competitive currency devaluations, exchange controls, collapsing trade and the political extremism that followed. The governing conviction, held on both sides of the Atlantic, was that open commerce and stable money were not merely prosperous but pacifying, and that leaving each country to defend its own balance of payments alone had helped wreck the previous peace.

The Fund's design emerged from a negotiation between two plans, one drafted by John Maynard Keynes for the British Treasury and one by Harry Dexter White for the American. Keynes wanted something closer to a world central bank, issuing its own reserve unit and pressing surplus countries as well as deficit ones to adjust; White wanted a more limited pool of national currencies under conditions the largest contributors could control. White's conception largely prevailed, as the balance of wartime power made likely. What resulted was a fund of member subscriptions, or quotas, that set both a country's contribution and its voting weight, from which members facing balance-of-payments trouble could draw short-term support rather than resorting to devaluation or import barriers. Members pledged to hold their currencies at declared par values, adjustable only in consultation with the Fund; the dollar was fixed to gold, and other currencies to the dollar.

Signing at Bretton Woods was not the same as existence. The Articles entered into force on 27 December 1945, once enough governments had ratified, the US Congress having authorized American participation that July. The Fund opened its doors and began operations in March 1947, and France made the first drawing that May. The Soviet delegation had attended the conference and its representatives negotiated over quotas, but Stalin declined to ratify, reportedly persuaded that the institution would be run from Washington — a judgement that fixed the Fund on one side of the Cold War almost from birth. The par value system it was built to police lasted until the early 1970s, when the United States ended dollar convertibility into gold; the Fund itself outlived the system, taking on new roles in lending, surveillance and, later, crisis management across the developing world.
significance: The 1944 agreement created something with no real precedent: a permanent, treaty-based body with standing authority to inspect and lend to sovereign states' economies in peacetime. Whatever one thinks of how the Fund has used that authority — and its structural adjustment programmes of the 1980s and 1990s remain fiercely contested — the institutional form has proved durable and much copied, and the idea that monetary policy is a matter of legitimate international consultation rather than purely national prerogative dates in practice from that hotel in New Hampshire. The quota system also embedded the economic hierarchy of 1944 into the machinery of global governance, giving the United States and Western Europe a weight in decisions that decolonized states spent the following decades trying, mostly unsuccessfully, to renegotiate.
coverage: The dataset holds no events at all beneath this story, so everything here comes from published reference and institutional accounts rather than from mapped incidents; the span given, 1944, marks only the conference, not the Fund's entry into force in 1945 or its opening in 1947. The documentary record of Bretton Woods itself is unusually rich — conference proceedings, Keynes's and White's papers, the IMF's own multi-volume histories — but it is dominated by the Anglo-American negotiation, and the aims and internal deliberations of the Soviet, Latin American, Chinese and Indian delegations are far less well covered in accessible English-language sources than their numerical presence at the conference would suggest.
